title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 4
paragraphs: We who didn't live through those days naturally picture them this way: half of Russia conquered, the inhabitants fleeing to distant provinces, one levy after another raised to defend the fatherland, and every Russian, great or small, busy only with sacrificing himself, saving his country or weeping over its fall. The tales and descriptions of that time, without exception, speak only of Russian self-sacrifice, patriotic devotion, despair, grief and heroism. But it was not really so. It looks that way to us because we see only the general historic interest of the time and miss the personal, human interests people actually had. Yet the personal interests of the moment are so much stronger than the general ones that they always stop the public interest from being felt or even noticed. Most people then paid no attention to the general course of events and followed only their private interests, and these were the very people whose activity in that period was the most useful.

The people who tried to understand the general course of events and join in it with self-sacrifice and heroism were the most useless members of society. They saw everything upside down, and everything they did for the common good turned out useless and foolish — like Pierre's and Mamonov's regiments, which looted Russian villages, or the lint the young ladies prepared that never reached the wounded, and so on. Even people who loved intellectual talk and expressing their feelings, and who discussed Russia's position at the time, could not help bringing into their talk either a touch of pretense and falsehood or pointless condemnation and anger aimed at people accused of things no one could possibly be guilty of. In historic events the ban on eating the fruit of the Tree of Knowledge applies with special force. Only unconscious action bears fruit, and whoever plays a part in a historic event never understands what it means. If he tries to understand it, his efforts come to nothing.

The more closely a man was involved in the events then taking place in Russia, the less he understood their significance. In Petersburg and in the provinces far from Moscow, ladies and gentlemen in militia uniforms wept for Russia and its ancient capital and talked of self-sacrifice and so on. But in the army that had retreated beyond Moscow there was little talk or thought of Moscow, and when the soldiers caught sight of its burned ruins, no one swore to take revenge on the French. They thought about their next pay, their next quarters, Matreshka the vivandière, and things of that sort.

The war had caught Nicholas Rostov in the service, so he took a close and lasting part in the defense of his country. But he did it casually, with no thought of self-sacrifice, and so he watched what was happening in Russia without despair and without gloomily racking his brains. Had anyone asked what he thought of the state of Russia, he would have answered that it was not his business to think about it; Kutuzov and others were there for that. He had heard, however, that the regiments were to be filled up to full strength, that the fighting would probably go on a long time yet, and that, such being the case, he might very well command a regiment in a couple of years.

Since he saw the matter this way, he felt no regret when he learned that he was being sent to Voronezh to buy remounts for his division, and so would miss the coming battle. He felt the greatest pleasure. He did not hide it, and his comrades understood it perfectly.
A few days before the battle of Borodino, Nicholas received the money and warrants he needed, sent some hussars ahead, and set out for Voronezh with post horses.

Only someone who has been through it, who has spent some months without a break in the atmosphere of campaigning and war, can understand how delighted Nicholas was to get out of the area stripped by the army's foraging parties and crowded with its supply trains and hospitals. Free of soldiers, wagons and the filthy traces of a camp, he saw villages with peasants and peasant women, country houses, fields with cattle grazing, posthouses with the stationmasters asleep, and he rejoiced as if seeing it all for the first time. What surprised and delighted him most, for a long while, were the women. They were young and healthy, with no dozen officers courting each one, and they were pleased and flattered when a passing officer joked with them.

In the highest spirits, Nicholas reached a hotel in Voronezh at night and ordered things he had long done without in camp. The next day, very clean-shaven and in a full-dress uniform he had not worn for a long time, he went to present himself to the authorities.

The militia commander was a civilian general, an old man who was clearly pleased with his military title and rank. He greeted Nicholas curtly (thinking that was how soldiers behaved) and questioned him with an air of importance, as though he were weighing the general state of affairs and had every right to approve and disapprove. Nicholas was in such high spirits that it only amused him.

From the commander of the militia he drove to the governor. The governor was a brisk little man, very simple and friendly. He named the stud farms where Nicholas could get horses, recommended a horse dealer in the town and a landowner fourteen miles out who had the best horses, and promised to help him in every way.

"You are Count Ilya Rostov's son? My wife was a great friend of your mother's. We are at home on Thursdays, and today is Thursday, so please come and see us quite informally," said the governor as he said goodbye.

Nicholas left the governor's, hired post horses at once, took his squadron quartermaster along and drove at a gallop to the landowner with the stud, fourteen miles off. In that first part of his stay in Voronezh everything seemed pleasant and easy to him, and, as usually happens when a man is in a pleasant mood, everything went well and easily.

The landowner Nicholas went to see was a bachelor, an old cavalryman, a horse lover and sportsman. He had some century-old brandy and old Hungarian wine, a snuggery where he smoked, and some splendid horses.

Nicholas bought seventeen picked stallions for six thousand rubles, with very little talk — to serve, as he put it, as samples of his remounts. After dinner, having taken rather too much of the Hungarian wine, he exchanged kisses with the landowner, with whom he was already on the friendliest terms, and galloped back over abominable roads in the brightest of moods. He kept urging the driver on so as to reach the governor's party in time.
He changed, poured water over his head and scented himself, and arrived at the governor's rather late, but with the phrase "better late than never" on his lips.

It was not a ball, and no dancing had been announced, but everyone knew that Catherine Petrovna would play waltzes and the écossaise on the clavichord and that there would be dancing, so everyone had come as if to a ball.

Provincial life in 1812 went on much as usual, except that it was livelier in the towns because many wealthy families had come from Moscow. A special recklessness showed in everything done in Russia then, an "in for a penny, in for a pound — who cares?" spirit. And the inevitable small talk now turned not on the weather and mutual acquaintances but on Moscow, the army and Napoleon.
The company gathered at the governor's was the best in Voronezh.

There were a great many ladies and a few of Nicholas' Moscow acquaintances, but no man there could in any way rival the cavalier of St. George, the hussar remount officer, the good-natured and well-bred Count Rostov. Among the men was an Italian prisoner, an officer in the French army, and Nicholas felt that the prisoner's presence added to his own importance as a Russian hero. The Italian was, as it were, a war trophy. Nicholas felt this, and it seemed to him that everyone saw the Italian the same way, so he treated him cordially, though with dignity and restraint.

As soon as Nicholas entered in his hussar uniform, spreading around him a fragrance of perfume and wine, said "better late than never" and heard others repeat it several times, people clustered around him. All eyes turned on him, and he felt at once that he had stepped into his proper position in the province, that of universal favorite. It was a very pleasant position, and intoxicatingly so after his long privations. At posting stations, at inns and in the landowner's snuggery, maidservants had been flattered by his notice, and here too at the governor's party there were (as it seemed to Nicholas) an inexhaustible number of pretty young women, married and unmarried, impatiently waiting for him to notice them. The women and girls flirted with him, and from the first day the people concerned set about getting this fine young daredevil of a hussar married and settled down. Among them was the governor's wife herself, who welcomed Rostov as a near relative and called him "Nicholas."

Catherine Petrovna did play waltzes and the écossaise, and the dancing began, and Nicholas won over provincial society still more with his agility. His unusually free way of dancing astonished them all. Nicholas was rather astonished at it himself that evening. He had never danced like that in Moscow, and he would have thought such a free and easy manner improper and in bad taste. But here he felt it was his duty to amaze them all with something out of the ordinary, something they would have to accept as the regular thing in the capital even though it was new to them in the provinces.

All evening Nicholas paid attention to a blue-eyed, plump and pleasing little blonde, the wife of one of the provincial officials. With the naive conviction of young men in a merry mood that other men's wives were created for them, Rostov did not leave the lady's side and treated her husband in a friendly, conspiratorial way, as if, without saying it, they both knew how splendidly Nicholas and the lady would get on together. The husband, however, did not seem to share that conviction and tried to behave morosely toward Rostov. But Nicholas' good-natured naivety was so boundless that sometimes even the husband gave way, in spite of himself, to Nicholas' good humor. Toward the end of the evening, though, as the wife's face grew more flushed and animated, the husband's grew more and more melancholy and solemn, as if there were only a fixed amount of animation between them, and as the wife's share grew, the husband's shrank.
